Stated Claim / Post Context:
‘Still alive and snoring’: Christa Pike’s attorneys file emergency motion to halt execution

Attorneys filed an emergency motion to halt the execution of Christa Pike in Tennessee after she was reported 'still alive and snoring' following lethal injection.

Actual Article Body:
NASHVILLE, Tenn. (WSMV/Gray News) – Tennessee officials were unable to put Christa Gail Pike to death Wednesday for a 1995 murder after administering two doses of a lethal drug.

Her attorneys have filed an emergency motion to halt her execution after they say Pike was “still alive and snoring” after receiving her lethal injection on Wednesday.

“The vein in my arm feels like it’s about to bust,” one witness recalled her saying.

According to the emergency motion, the Tennessee Department of Correction began the execution of Pike at about 9 p.m. ET. The motion says that both syringes of pentobarbital were administered and that Pike “has not lost consciousness and still has a heartbeat and is audibly snoring.”

“It sounded like she was almost choking,” the witness recalled.

The emergency motion filed Wednesday night stated the execution is “causing Ms. Pike unnecessary agony and occurring in violation of [her] right to be executed free of cruel and unusual punishment.”

The motion also demanded the Tennessee Department of Correction immediately begin lifesaving measures.

The 50-year-old inmate was taken by ambulance from the prison, her attorneys said. She was being treated at a hospital.

“Tonight the State of Tennessee once again failed to carry out a lawful execution,” they said. “We take no pleasure in being right, but the concerns raised by Ms. Pike proved to be true: difficult vein access, blown veins, degraded pentobarbital, no emergency medical care available when things inevitably go wrong, all under a protocol that remains veiled in secrecy.”

As of 11:40 p.m. ET, they said they had not been informed about her condition.

Pike had been scheduled for execution at 10 a.m. Wednesday for the killing she committed at age 18 and would have been the first woman executed in Tennessee in more than 200 years.

An appeals court stopped the lethal injection just an hour before it was to start, and hours later the U.S. Supreme Court overturned that stay.
